results.quote: Aurignacian, about 43,000–33,000 years ago, is the first Upper Palaeolithic technocomplex
results.claim: The Aurignacian dates to approximately 43,000–33,000 years ago and is the first Upper Palaeolithic technocomplex to spread across most of Europe

results.quote: Hohle Fels female figurine, carved from mammoth ivory, is at least 35,000 years old
results.claim: The Hohle Fels female figurine is at least 35,000 years old

results.quote: Most Aurignacian marks, however, are not figurative. They are notches, lines, dots and crosses
results.claim: Most Aurignacian marks are non-figurative notches, lines, dots, and crosses on tools, ornaments, and stone blocks

results.quote: Repeated sequences of such marks have been read as possible notational or information-storage devices
results.claim: Repeated sequences of Aurignacian marks have been interpreted as possible notational or information-storage devices

results.quote: If they were shared conventions, their repertoires might differ between regions, as personal ornaments do
results.claim: If Aurignacian marks were shared conventions, their sign repertoires might differ between regions, similar to personal ornaments

results.quote: Using SignBase (Dutkiewicz et al., 2020), I ask whether sign repertoires differ between Germany and France
results.claim: The study uses SignBase to test whether sign repertoires differ between Germany and France

results.quote: SignBase v1.0 (Bentz et al., 2020) records 531 Aurignacian mobile objects from 65 sites in 13 countries
results.claim: SignBase v1.0 contains 531 Aurignacian mobile objects from 65 sites across 13 countries

results.quote: with 31 binary columns for the presence of each sign type
results.claim: SignBase records presence/absence data for 31 sign types as binary columns

results.quote: Germany (n = 264) and France (n = 148) provide most records
results.claim: Germany contributes 264 objects and France contributes 148 objects to SignBase

results.quote: restricted the analysis to these two countries and removed duplicate records
results.claim: The analysis is restricted to Germany and France with duplicate records removed

results.quote: calculated the proportion of objects carrying each sign type in each country and counted the objects from each site
results.claim: The study calculates per-country proportions of objects carrying each sign type and counts objects per site

results.quote: The analysed sample contains 108 objects (46 German, 62 French)
results.claim: After removing duplicates, the analysed sample contains 108 objects: 46 from Germany and 62 from France

results.quote: The most frequent sign type is notch in Germany and notch in France
results.claim: Notches are the most frequent sign type in both Germany and France

results.quote: The German objects come from 9 sites and the French objects from 21
results.claim: German objects in the analysed sample come from 9 sites; French objects come from 21 sites

results.quote: Figure 1 shows how the common sign types are spread across these sites
results.claim: Figure 1 displays the distribution of the ten most common sign types across sites in Germany and France

results.quote: Number of objects at each site carrying each of the ten most common sign types
results.claim: Figure 1 shows the number of objects at each site carrying each of the ten most common sign types

results.quote: Sites are ordered by their total number of analysed objects; sites with none of these sign types are not shown
results.claim: In Figure 1, sites are ordered by total analysed objects and sites lacking the top 10 sign types are excluded

results.quote: Vogelherd alone supplies 30% of the German objects, and Castanet supplies 13% of the French ones
results.claim: Vogelherd contributes 30% of German objects and Castanet contributes 13% of French objects in the analysed sample

results.quote: a national difference may reflect the excavation and preservation history of a few sites
results.claim: Observed national differences in sign repertoires may reflect excavation and preservation biases at a few dominant sites

results.quote: Objects from the same layer are not independent, so sites rather than objects are the better unit of comparison
results.claim: Objects from the same archaeological layer are not statistically independent; sites are the appropriate unit of comparison

results.quote: Germany and France share their common sign types and differ only in rare ones
results.claim: Germany and France share the same common sign types; differences appear only in rare sign types

results.quote: Notches and lines are the two most frequent signs in both countries
results.claim: Notches and lines are the two most frequent sign types in both Germany and France

results.quote: Notches appear on 57% of German objects and 45% of French objects
results.claim: Notches appear on 57% of German objects and 45% of French objects

results.quote: lines on 35% and 35%
results.claim: Lines appear on 35% of German objects and 35% of French objects

results.quote: oblique lines occur on 15% of German objects but 2% of French ones
results.claim: Oblique lines occur on 15% of German objects but only 2% of French objects

results.quote: vulva signs appear only in France, on 8% of French objects
results.claim: Vulva signs appear only in France, on 8% of French objects

results.quote: Three sites (Vogelherd, Hohle Fels, and Geissenklösterle) supply 80% of the German objects
results.claim: Three German sites (Vogelherd, Hohle Fels, Geissenklösterle) supply 80% of German objects in the sample

results.quote: these few rare-sign contrasts do not yet show separate regional traditions
results.claim: The rare-sign differences between Germany and France do not demonstrate separate regional traditions
